body:
The economic setting of the Early Vedic Period

The Early Vedic Period, conventionally dated to about 1500–1000 BCE, was associated mainly with the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent, including the Punjab region and areas around the Indus and its tributaries. The Rigveda provides important information about the livelihoods of communities living in this region.

The economy was predominantly pastoral, meaning that the rearing of domesticated animals formed a major part of economic life. Cattle were especially important, but people also kept other animals and cultivated crops. The term agro-pastoral economy describes this combination of agriculture and animal husbandry.

Pastoralism and agriculture

Pastoralism is the rearing of livestock for food and other economic purposes. Agriculture is the cultivation of crops. Early Vedic communities practised both, although cattle rearing occupied a particularly prominent position.

Why cattle were considered wealth

Cattle had several economic uses. Cows supplied milk, from which products such as curd and ghee could be prepared. Oxen provided animal power for agricultural work and transport. Cattle could also be exchanged or presented as valuable gifts.

The importance of cattle is reflected in the Rigveda's prayers for livestock and in accounts of conflicts over herds. The term gavishti, literally associated with the search for cows, is traditionally used to illustrate the connection between cattle and conflict in early Vedic society.

Possession of large herds could indicate prosperity because livestock represented productive resources as well as valuable property. Cattle were therefore more than a source of food.

Horses, transport and animal power

Horses were important, particularly in connection with chariots and warfare. Rigvedic hymns refer to horses, chariots and carts. Oxen, by contrast, were especially useful for pulling loads and performing agricultural work.

These uses should not be confused. The importance of horse-drawn chariots in warfare does not mean that horses were the principal animals used for ploughing.

Pasture, water and cultivation

Livestock required grazing land and access to water. Consequently, control over pastures and water sources had economic importance. The Rigveda describes conflicts fought to capture cattle and to obtain land or water.

Land was valuable for more than grazing. People also grew crops, particularly barley. This meant that a community could depend on both herds and fields. The balance between these activities varied according to local conditions.

Movement in search of grazing resources was compatible with the existence of settlements and cultivated fields. It would therefore be misleading to describe every early Vedic community as completely nomadic or entirely dependent on cattle.

Wealth and its distribution

Wealth obtained through conflict could be distributed among leaders, priests and other members of the community. Cattle and other valuable goods were also presented as gifts.

These arrangements differed from the more regular taxation systems of later territorial kingdoms. The Rigvedic raja was primarily a community leader and did not normally maintain the elaborate tax-collecting machinery associated with later states.

Prelims focus

  • The Early Vedic Period is conventionally placed at about 1500–1000 BCE.
  • Its principal geographical setting was the northwestern subcontinent.
  • Cattle rearing was especially important, but cultivation was also practised.
  • Gavishti is associated with the search for cattle and the economic importance of cattle-related conflict.
  • Horses were important for chariots, while oxen supplied power for transport and cultivation.
  • Trap: A predominantly pastoral economy was not an economy without agriculture.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, 'What Books and Burials Tell Us', printed pp. 43–47; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Outlines of Indian History, 'Vedic Culture', section 5.4, 'Economy' (consulted 17 November 2026).]

title: Cattle and the Early Vedic Pastoral Economy

body:
Agriculture became increasingly important

During the Later Vedic Period, conventionally dated to about 1000–600 BCE, cultivation became more important in many communities of northern India. This development accompanied the growth of more settled villages and the expansion of settlements from the northwest towards the Ganga-Yamuna region.

The distinction between the 2 phases is one of relative economic emphasis. Early Vedic communities already cultivated crops, while later Vedic communities continued to rear cattle. Agriculture did not suddenly begin in 1000 BCE, and pastoralism did not disappear.

Crops and food production

Barley, commonly identified with the Vedic term yava, was an important cereal in early Vedic life. Wheat was also known. As cultivation expanded into different environments, rice became increasingly important, particularly in areas favourable to its growth.

Settlements associated with the janapadas provide evidence of a wider agricultural economy. Crops grown at such settlements included rice, wheat, barley, pulses, sugarcane, sesame and mustard.

These crops should not all be treated as equally important everywhere or throughout the entire Vedic Period. Crop selection depended on rainfall, soil, water availability and local practices.

Ploughing and the importance of oxen

Plough agriculture involves using a plough to loosen and turn soil before sowing. Oxen could supply the power required to pull a plough. Their use connected animal husbandry directly with crop production.

Wooden agricultural implements continued to be used even as iron technology spread. The growing use of iron did not mean that every cultivator immediately acquired an iron ploughshare.

More sustained cultivation encouraged investment of labour in fields, the management of livestock and the storage of harvested grain. Where production exceeded immediate household needs, part of the produce could support people engaged in other occupations.

Soil, rainfall and agricultural methods

Different agricultural environments required different methods. The fertile alluvial soils of river valleys could support substantial cultivation, but the choice of implement depended on soil conditions and available resources.

From around the 6th century BCE, the use of iron-tipped ploughshares became increasingly significant in suitable high-rainfall areas, including parts of the Ganga valley. Such implements could turn heavy soil more effectively. Their advantages were not identical in dry or hilly regions, where other agricultural methods remained suitable.

Rice transplantation and irrigation

Transplantation of paddy involves raising young rice plants and then moving them to prepared wet fields. This differs from scattering seeds directly in a field. Where sufficient water and labour were available, transplantation could improve the survival of young plants and increase yields.

This technique required considerable labour. Its growing importance is particularly associated with agricultural intensification in parts of the Ganga valley from about the 6th century BCE, during the period of early states. It should not be presented as a universal feature of early Rigvedic farming.

Water management also became increasingly important. Wells and tanks, and less commonly canals, supported cultivation in suitable areas. Irrigation could reduce dependence on uncertain rainfall, although it did not remove the need for favourable local conditions.

Economic consequences of greater cultivation

In favourable areas, more dependable or productive cultivation could support larger settlements and a greater variety of occupations. A portion of agricultural output could be consumed by craftspeople, traders and other people who were not primarily engaged in growing food.

However, increased production did not automatically create cities. Settlement growth also depended on exchange, labour organisation, political authority and regional circumstances.

Prelims focus

  • The Later Vedic Period is conventionally dated to about 1000–600 BCE.
  • Barley was an important early Vedic cereal; rice became increasingly significant in suitable eastern regions.
  • Oxen provided animal power for plough agriculture.
  • From about the 6th century BCE, iron ploughshares were increasingly useful in suitable heavy alluvial soils.
  • Paddy transplantation could improve crop survival but required sufficient water and substantial labour.
  • Trap: Neither iron ploughing nor transplantation was adopted uniformly throughout the subcontinent.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, printed p. 46, and Chapter 6, 'Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic', printed pp. 56–60; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', section 5.2, 'Strategies for Increasing Production', printed pp. 38–39; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Outlines of Indian History, 'Vedic Culture', sections 5.4 and 6.3 (consulted 17 November 2026).]

title: Agriculture and the Growth of Settled Cultivation

body:
The spread of iron-working

Iron technology became an increasingly important feature of the first millennium BCE in different parts of the Indian subcontinent. Its adoption was gradual and varied by region. Iron tools appeared alongside implements made from other materials rather than replacing them everywhere at once.

The distinction between metals mentioned in Vedic texts is important. The Rigvedic word ayas is generally understood in its early context as referring to copper or bronze rather than automatically to iron. Later Vedic expressions such as krishna ayas, meaning dark metal, are commonly associated with iron.

Do not equate every reference to ayas with iron

The occurrence of ayas in an early text is not, by itself, proof of iron-working. The terminology and the period in which it was used must be considered together.

How iron tools affected work

Iron could be shaped into tools with strong cutting edges. As iron-working became more established, it provided useful implements for several activities.

  • Axes: Useful for cutting wood and clearing vegetation where land was being brought under cultivation.
  • Ploughshares: Iron-tipped ploughshares could help turn heavy soils more effectively than some wooden implements.
  • Sickles and other cutting tools: Useful for harvesting and associated agricultural work.
  • Weapons: Iron could also be used for weapons, including spearheads and arrowheads.

The availability of a new tool did not guarantee greater agricultural output. Farmers also needed suitable land, sufficient water, access to animals or labour and the ability to obtain or maintain the implement.

The growing use of iron axes and ploughshares is particularly visible in the period approaching and following the 6th century BCE. It contributed to agricultural change in some regions, but the development of larger settlements cannot be attributed to iron alone.

Painted Grey Ware and northern settlements

Painted Grey Ware (PGW) is a distinctive type of pottery associated with settlements in parts of northern India, particularly the upper Ganga-Yamuna region. It is commonly connected with the later Vedic and early Iron Age setting, although its precise date range varies among sites.

PGW vessels are generally fine grey pottery decorated with dark painted designs such as lines and geometric patterns. Bowls and plates are among their characteristic forms.

Important sites associated with PGW include Hastinapura near Meerut, Atranjikhera near Etah in Uttar Pradesh, and Purana Qila in Delhi. These settlements also provide evidence for village life, livestock and cultivation.

Distinguishing PGW from later fine pottery

PotteryIdentifying featureBroad historical association
Painted Grey Ware (PGW)Grey vessels with dark painted lines or geometric designsLater Vedic and early Iron Age settlements, especially in northern India
Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW)Fine pottery with a distinctive glossy, often black, polished surfaceGrowing towns and the early historic economy, especially from around the 6th century BCE onward

The names describe types of pottery, not the names of political kingdoms or separate ethnic groups. PGW and NBPW also overlapped in time at some sites. Their appearance should therefore not be treated as a single nationwide change that occurred in one year.

Iron and pottery belong to a wider economic change

The spread of iron-working and the presence of characteristic pottery help distinguish changing material conditions in some settlements. These developments occurred alongside agriculture, animal husbandry and craft production.

Other parts of the subcontinent had different pottery traditions and patterns of iron use. A type found prominently in the Ganga-Yamuna region should not be assumed to characterise every contemporary settlement in India.

Prelims focus

  • Krishna ayas is associated with iron in later Vedic terminology.
  • The earlier term ayas should not automatically be translated as iron.
  • Iron axes, ploughshares, sickles and weapons had different practical uses.
  • PGW: Fine grey pottery with painted designs; associated with the upper Ganga-Yamuna region.
  • Hastinapura, Atranjikhera and Purana Qila are important PGW-associated sites.
  • Trap: PGW is not the same as the later, glossy Northern Black Polished Ware.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 6, printed pp. 56–57, and Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed p. 87; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Michel Danino, 'Technology in Ancient India', sections 2–3; Ravi Korisettar and Arjun Rao, 'Iron Age – Society and Economy', sections 4–7 (both consulted 17 November 2026).]

title: Iron Technology, Agricultural Tools and Painted Grey Ware

body:
Crafts formed part of the rural economy

Vedic economic life was not limited to herding and cultivation. People also produced useful goods from clay, fibres, wood and metals. These activities are called crafts.

Vedic texts mention occupations such as agriculturists, weavers, potters, builders and carpenters. They also refer to other kinds of specialised work. This indicates that communities depended on a range of skills rather than on every household producing all its requirements independently.

Some production could take place within households, while particular people developed greater skill in certain crafts. The balance between household work and specialised occupations varied among communities and over time.

Pottery and the use of clay

Potters shaped clay into containers and other vessels needed for storing, preparing and serving food. Pottery was especially useful in settled communities because households required durable containers for grain, water and daily activities.

Different pottery traditions appeared in different regions and periods. Painted Grey Ware, associated with parts of northern India during the later Vedic and early Iron Age setting, is one example of specialised pottery production.

Fine pottery should be distinguished from ordinary household vessels. Both could be useful, but their forms, finishes and possible uses were not necessarily identical.

Weaving and textile production

Weaving turns thread or yarn into cloth by interlacing fibres. The production of textiles required knowledge of preparing fibres, making thread and weaving fabric.

Textiles supplied clothing and other useful materials. Weaving could be performed as household work, while skilled producers could also make goods for exchange.

The existence of weaving as an occupation does not imply that large organised textile workshops or later urban merchant associations already existed in every Vedic village.

Carpentry and metalworking

Carpenters worked with timber to make useful objects such as carts, parts of buildings and agricultural implements. Their work was linked to transport, settlement construction and cultivation.

Metalworkers produced objects from available metals. Copper and bronze were known before the widespread adoption of iron. As iron-working expanded, smiths could make and repair additional kinds of tools and weapons.

Wooden and metal components often served different functions. For example, a plough could have a wooden structure while a later iron-tipped ploughshare provided a stronger working edge. The use of iron therefore expanded the range of available materials rather than making wood unnecessary.

Why craft specialisation mattered

Craft production connected different economic activities. Farmers needed tools, containers and transport equipment. Craftspeople needed food and raw materials. Herders supplied animal products and could contribute to transport.

As settled cultivation expanded, some communities could support a greater range of skilled workers. Finished goods could be used locally, given as gifts or exchanged with others.

These connections explain why agriculture, pastoralism and crafts developed together. They were related parts of economic life rather than completely separate occupations.

Prelims focus

  • Vedic texts mention occupations including weavers, potters, builders and carpenters.
  • Pottery supplied useful vessels for household and settlement needs.
  • Weaving involved the production of cloth from thread or yarn.
  • Carpentry supported transport, construction and agriculture.
  • Copper and bronze continued to be used as iron-working expanded.
  • Trap: The presence of crafts does not establish the existence of the fully developed guild system associated with later towns.

[Sources: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'India’s Cultural Roots', section 'Vedic Society', printed p. 109; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 6, printed pp. 55–57, and Chapter 9, printed pp. 89–94; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Outlines of Indian History, 'Vedic Culture', section 5.4, and Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, 'Technology in Ancient India', sections 2–3 (consulted 17 November 2026).]
